items.item: A map task's single data file is produced by the sort-based shuffle writer: records are buffered, sorted by target reduce partition (spilling to disk if memory runs out), then written once as one sorted, consolidated file.

at.step: Reveal: one pair per map task

items.item: The index file's size depends only on the number of reduce partitions (one offset entry each), never on data volume — this is why index bytes stay small relative to data bytes at every scale this topic measures.

at.out: measured directly in examples.py (total_index_bytes < total_data_bytes); not separately dramatised as its own reel step

items.item: The MapOutputTracker lives on the driver and is itself just a registry: map task ID to (executor, offsets-within-file) for every shuffle; a reducer's very first action before any fetch is a request to this registry, not a blind guess at executor addresses.

at.step: Reveal: how a reducer finds its blocks

items.item: A reducer's ShuffleBlockFetcherIterator bounds how many blocks it requests concurrently (spark.reducer.maxReqsInFlight-style limits) precisely because an unbounded fan-out of small block requests, M times R of them, would itself overwhelm a map-side executor's connections.

Logical block count is exactly M times R (every map task's file has one span for every reduce partition), which is why both disk I/O and network fetch overhead grow multiplicatively, not additively, as either dimension scales — the chapter's recurring 'small blocks' cost driver.

at.step: Reveal: blocks scale as M times R

items.item: Serialisation cost is paid twice per block that crosses the network: once on the map side writing it, once on the reduce side reading it back — named in the recap's cost list but not separately measured by this topic's own examples.py.

at.out: serialisation cost is named, not independently benchmarked; deferred to this chapter's own later performance-tuning topic if one exists

items.item: Spark 3+'s shuffle service and the push-based shuffle feature (server-side merge of small blocks before fetch) directly target the O(M×R) small-block cost this topic names, by reducing the number of distinct network requests a reducer must issue — a forward pointer, not built here.

at.out: shuffle service / push-based shuffle is a named frontier, this chapter's own later topic or out of scope entirely

items.item: Deleting and recreating a local shuffle directory mid-session (rather than letting Spark's BlockManager keep using the one it already initialised) crashes the next shuffle write with a FileNotFoundException — a real debugging finding from this topic's own examples.py, not a documented Spark behaviour, kept as a disclosed methodology note rather than a syllabus claim.

at.out: methodology-only; disclosed in FACT-CHECK.md, not a syllabus clause

items.item: A sort-based shuffle writer differs from the older hash-based shuffle writer (removed in Spark 2.0) precisely in writing one consolidated sorted file per map task instead of one file per (map task, reduce partition) pair — the historical reason the current scheme avoids an O(M×R) file-count explosion even though block count itself is still O(M×R).

at.out: named only as historical contrast; hash-based shuffle predates Spark 4.x and is not independently sourced here

items.item: Spill thresholds (spark.shuffle.spill, the memory fraction before a map task's sort buffer writes partial output to disk) determine how many intermediate spill files one map task produces before its final merge pass — the merge is what collapses those spills back into the single consolidated data file this topic names, not a separate persistent cost.

at.out: spill-threshold tuning is named only as a mechanism detail; not independently measured by this topic's own examples.py
